title: ijf-contest-shape
description: The contest-level half of the IJF aggregation, generated by tools/ijf-results alongside ijf-technique-frequency.json and never edited by hand. The frequency file answers how often a technique scores; this answers questions about the contest around the score - where in the draw it was won, which techniques end contests rather than only scoring in them, what athletes are penalised for, how long a division's contests last, and what is thrown when the clock is running out.

stats_from_year.description: The earliest year that reaches a ranking. The crawl goes back further than this on purpose: the IJF published its footage to YouTube until about 2022 and to its own subscription player afterwards, so older contests are where the freely watchable video is, while event tagging is unreliable before 2020. A ranking needs reliable tagging; a clip only needs to exist and be watchable. Contests older than this contribute their footage and nothing else.

excluded.description: What the aggregation left out, recorded rather than silently dropped. paralympic_contests counts contests excluded because they are visually impaired judo: Paralympic Games Tokyo 2020 is the only VI event in the IJF's feed carrying results, and across its 39 contests not one event carries a technique tag, so it can contribute no score and only makes the tagging rates it touches look worse. That the IJF publishes no technique data for VI judo is a finding, and it should not be discoverable only by noticing an absence.

pre_window_contests.description: Contests read for their clips alone, being older than stats_from_year.

rounds.description: What scores, by how deep in the draw the contest was. Medal-round judo against preliminary judo.

conversion.description: Scored with this technique and won the contest, against scored with it and lost. The difference between a technique that puts points on the board and one that finishes contests. Counts scores, not contests: a contest with three scores contributes three times.

outcomes.description: How contests in a category end, and how long they take. no_contest is a walkover or withdrawal: no score, no penalty decision, and nobody on the mat.

seconds_p50.description: Median contest length in seconds, over contests that actually happened. Null where none did.

penalties.description: Every penalty given, by what it was for and when. Not only the penalty that ended the contest: a shido that cost nothing still says what a referee in this category is watching for. `reason` is the IJF's own code, kept untranslated so the table stays theirs.

countries.description: What each country scores with. Weight and tier are deliberately dropped from the slice: the question is national style, the cells would otherwise be too thin to mean anything, and a narrower slice is one step closer to identifying a person.

first_score.description: Whether the athlete who scored first went on to win, by when they scored it. Scoring first in the opening minute and scoring first in golden score are different propositions.

response.description: What it costs to score. NOT a counter-attack rate: judo restarts from standing after a score, so the opponent's answer is the next exchange rather than a counter to the throw that landed. What it measures is whether scoring with a technique tends to invite an immediate reply. `continued` counts only scores the contest carried on past, since an ippon cannot be answered; `answered_fast` is within 30 seconds of contest clock, which is this project's judgement and not an IJF definition.

trailing.description: What scores in the closing minute and in golden score, by what the scoreboard said the moment before it landed. Only minute 4 and golden score are recorded, because that is the question: what works when you are behind and running out of contest. State is read from waza-ari on the board, which is the only score that accumulates.

examples.description: One technique, in one division, as it was actually done: up to two contests per technique per weight class, because "seen in competition" is only useful if it is seen in YOUR division. Ranked watchable first (the IJF moved its footage off YouTube around 2023 and its own player needs a subscription, so a free clip is preferred even when older), then ippon, then most recent.

contest.description: The IJF's contest_code_long, which is the path segment JudoBase routes on: judobase.ijf.org/#/competition/contest/<contest>. Works for every contest whatever platform holds its footage, and sends a reader to the IJF's own site rather than reproducing anything.

competition.description: The competition's own name, for the caption. What to call a clip now that it is not called after anybody: the occasion and the outcome do the work a competitor's name would have done.

platform.description: The IJF's own code: yt for YouTube, yawebtv for its own player.

seconds.description: Where the throw sits in the recording, as media start + time_real + video_offset. time_real is wall clock including every matte stoppage, which is why it and not the contest clock matches video position. Lands about five seconds BEFORE the throw, deliberately: someone learning a technique needs the grip fight and the entry, not the landing. Verified against real footage on gs_isr2022_m_p100_0023.

round.description: Read from round_name, never from the numeric round: that field is a draw-structure index, not a depth, and carries "Bronze", "Final" and "Round 1" under the same number.

technique.description: Waza Book slug. Null only in the importer's permissive mode, which must not be committed.
